Projections

The violet years on the timeline are projections. We made them with a linear regression: a straight line of best fit through the last 30 years of measurements, continued to 2100.

How It Works

  1. Take the last 30 years. For the place and layer you picked, we use its 30 most recent measured years.
  2. Fit a straight line. Linear regression finds the line that sits closest to those 30 points. Its slope is the “trend per decade” shown in the atlas.
  3. Continue the line to 2100. The dashed violet line is that same line carried forward. The shaded area is where we expect 95% of future years to land, and it widens the further ahead you look.

Two small adjustments keep it sensible. If a place’s trend is weak compared with its normal year-to-year swings, the line is flattened toward the recent average, so noise is not projected as change. And because real years never sit exactly on a line, the map shows one possible year with typical swings added.

Reliability

We tested the method on the past: start it in an earlier year, give it only the 30 years before, and compare its projection with what was later measured. Across every layer, 93–98% of the later measurements fell inside the shaded range, so the range is reliable.

However, the projected line should be treated as a rough guide, not a precise prediction. When looking at temperature, the trend performed only slightly better than assuming no change, while for the other environmental variables, it offered no meaningful improvement.

As projections extend further into the future, uncertainty increases. Around 2050 and beyond, the range of possible outcomes becomes more informative than the projected line itself.

By 2100, the uncertainty range is approximately ±0.9 °C for the global average and about ±3.6 °C for a typical single grid cell, implying that global trends are generally more stable than estimates for individual locations.

Understanding Our Projections

Our projections extend historical climate trends into the future, assuming the observed rate of change continues. It should be noted that this is not an all encompassing climate model, and should not be treated as such. In other words, our projections are useful for exploring historical trends and understanding what could happen if current patterns continue, but they should not be treated as predictions of actual future climate conditions. For decisions that matter, use published climate-model projections such as those assessed by the IPCC. See our data & methods page for information about our datasets, calculations, and statistical methods.
